mappings.note: A pre-reading prompt asking what images of India come to the learner's own mind. Personal expression, C-E1.2; nothing is drawn from the text.
Requires background understanding of which regions carry French and Portuguese influence - conceptual understanding rather than an opinion or a fact from the chapter, so C-E1.1.
What the elders miss is stated in the opening paragraph; retrieval, LO-1.
'How do you know' forces the learner to cite the signs in the text (mixers, moulders, surviving furnaces) - textual evidence, LO-3.
'Pader' is named in the text; single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
Both halves are narrated - twice a day, and the bread-bangles the children wanted. Retrieval, LO-1.
Matches occasions to the bread each requires, all listed in the text. Extraction, LO-1.
The remembered fragrance of the loaves is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Accounts recorded in pencil on a wall is a stated detail; retrieval, LO-1.
That the sons continue the trade is stated; retrieval, LO-1.

Compares Rodrigues's evocative account with an impersonal one and asks what makes them different though the facts match - a question about a writer's treatment and style, which only C-E1.4 covers here.
Write your own descriptive account of a place, deliberately unlike an impersonal brochure. Style and tone are the marked skills, C-E1.2.
A group information-gathering task written up for the class. Composition and presentation, C-E1.2; nothing is extracted from the chapter.
Extract item on the kabai, the half-pant jibe and the monthly bills; every part is answered from the supplied passage. Retrieval, LO-1.
Elaborating on the baker as 'friend, companion and guide' means reading his place in the community - character and context, LO-2.
Same quotation, asked explicitly 'in relation to the character of the baker', which is LO-2.
'Justify the opinion' requires the answer to be built from what the chapter shows - textual evidence, LO-3, rather than free opinion under C-E1.2.
Lists the occasions the text ties to bread (Christmas, engagements, marriages). Extraction, LO-1.
The 'how do you know this' wording makes evidence the point of the question, LO-3, not the list itself.
Timing of the baker's rounds and the children's reason for running out are both narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
The bakers' prosperity has to be inferred from their plump 'jackfruit' physique and the trade's standing - reading the context, LO-2.
Names the varieties of bread and the occasions each belongs to, all stated in the text. Retrieval, LO-1.
Two stated descriptions of the baker's dress at two periods; extraction, LO-1.
Who attracts the 'dressed like a pader' jibe, and why, is spelt out in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Duplicate of the monthly-accounts item; a stated detail, LO-1.
Glosses the comparison 'jackfruit-like appearance' as a plump build. Interpreting an expression, C-E1.1.
A true/false comprehension check against the text (paders did not starve). Checking statements against stated content, LO-1.
Duplicate of the 'how do you know' item; the evidence requirement makes it LO-3.
Labels the tone of sentences from the text (matter-of-fact, nostalgic, funny, hopeful). Tone is an element of craft and no LO in this frame names it, so C-E1.4.
Fills a table of stated details about the baker (LO-1) and then turns the notes into a paragraph, which is composition (C-E1.2).
Reasons the baker was essential and what he wore are both listed in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Asks what reasons the WRITER gives, so the support is already in the text and is extracted; LO-1, not the learner-supplied evidence of LO-3.
Why the furnace was essential is answered by the list of occasions in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
What Rodrigues remembers 'fondly' is about the writer's own feeling towards the past, LO-2, rather than a neutral list.
'What lesson do you learn from their life' asks for the learner's own reflection, so C-E1.2 rather than a comprehension outcome.
Requires spotting which statement the extract does NOT support - a comprehension check against the supplied passage, LO-1.
Parts i and ii gloss 'time-tested' and 'the fire has not been extinguished' (C-E1.1); a further part asks for the author's tone, which is craft and belongs to C-E1.4.
Three parts retrieve what happened at the door and what the basket held (LO-1); the last asks which description fits the extract, i.e. its form and tone (C-E1.4).
Asks what 'he used to come at least twice a day' indicates about the baker's trade - an inference about context, LO-2, since the text never states the reason.
The baker's continuing place in village life is answered from the stated occasions; retrieval, LO-1.
